```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96,
                      fig.retina = 2, message = FALSE)
```

When the same model describes many individuals, subjects, cells or cell lines, their parameters
differ but are not unrelated. A mixed-effects model writes each individual parameter as a
population value plus a random deviation, estimates the population values and the spread of the
deviations, and integrates the deviations out of the likelihood. dMod2 builds such a model from
the same parts as any other, with the random effects declared in the `parfn`, and fits it with
`em()`.

The integral over the random effects, the marginal likelihood, has no closed form for an ODE
model. The four methods of `em()` approximate it in different ways, and all of them are instances
of the EM algorithm: FOCEI by Laplace's method at the modes of the random effects, adaptive
sparse-grid quadrature by a cubature rule around them, Laplace EM by an ECM iteration on the
Laplace approximation, and SAEM by Monte Carlo draws averaged over the iterations. This chapter
derives them, describes their settings, and fits each to the theophylline data set:
twelve subjects, one oral dose each, plasma concentrations over a day.

```{r}
library(dMod2)
options(dMod2.outdir = file.path(tempdir(), "guide-mixed-effects"))
dir.create(getOption("dMod2.outdir"), showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## Model

The dose goes into a depot and is absorbed into the central compartment of volume $V$, from which
it is cleared. The amount in the depot is a state of its own, in a frame of volume 1. The
absorption is a flux $k_a A_g$ out of the depot; arriving in the central compartment it is
divided by $V$. Elimination is written as a flux $\mathrm{Cl}\, C_c$ in the unit frame, so the
clearance $\mathrm{Cl}$ keeps its pharmacokinetic meaning, a volume per time, and the
concentration falls at the rate $\mathrm{Cl}/V$.

```{r}
reactions <- eqnlist() |>
  assignCompartment(Ag = "depot") |>
  assignCompartment(Cc = "central", volume = "V") |>
  setCompartmentVolume(unit = "1") |>
  addReaction("Ag", "Cc", "Ka * Ag", "absorption") |>
  addReaction("Cc", "", "Cl * Cc", "elimination", rateCompartment = "unit")
as.eqnvec(reactions)
```

`em()` needs second derivatives for its volume term and its reported Hessian, so the model parts
are built with `deriv2 = TRUE` and with the derivative modes that compute them by forward over
reverse sweeps.

```{r}
dm <- c("forward", "reverse", "forward-reverse")
x <- Xs(odemodel(reactions, modelname = "theo", compile = FALSE, deriv2 = TRUE, derivMode = dm))
g <- Y(c(cp = "Cc"), x, modelname = "theo_g", compile = FALSE, deriv2 = TRUE, derivMode = dm)
e <- Y(c(cp = "sigma"), g, attachInput = FALSE, modelname = "theo_e", compile = FALSE, deriv2 = TRUE,
       derivMode = dm)
```

## Data

Every subject is a condition. The table of conditions holds what differs between them, here
the dose in mg and the body weight.

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
data(Theoph, package = "datasets")
Theoph$Subject <- as.character(Theoph$Subject)
data <- as.datalist(data.frame(name = "cp", time = Theoph$Time, value = Theoph$conc, sigma = NA_real_,
                               condition = Theoph$Subject))
subjects <- sort(unique(Theoph$Subject))
table <- data.frame(ID = subjects, dose = tapply(Theoph$Dose * Theoph$Wt, Theoph$Subject, `[`, 1)[subjects],
                    weight = tapply(Theoph$Wt, Theoph$Subject, `[`, 1)[subjects], row.names = subjects)
head(table)
plotData(data) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "time [h]", y = "concentration [mg/L]", colour = "Subject")
```

## Random effects

`branch()` copies the transformation once per row of the table, and `insert()` makes it differ
between the subjects: the dose fills the depot, the central compartment starts empty, and the
parameters are on a log scale. An effect formula then turns a symbol into a linear predictor with
fixed and random effects, written as in lme4:

```{r}
trafo <- branch(define(NULL, "x <- x", x = c("Ka", "V", "Cl", "Ag", "Cc", "sigma")), table = table) |>
  insert("Ag <- dose", dose = dose) |>
  insert("Cc <- 0") |>
  insert("x <- exp(x)", x = c("Ka", "V", "Cl", "sigma")) |>
  insert(Ka + V + Cl ~ 1 + (1 | ID))
p <- P(trafo, method = "explicit", modelname = "theo_p", compile = FALSE, deriv2 = TRUE, derivMode = dm)
compile(x, g, e, p, output = "theo")
random <- randomEffects(p)
random
```

Since the formula acts after the log transformation, $\log \mathrm{Cl}_i = \mathrm{Cl} +
\eta_{\mathrm{Cl},i}$ with $\eta_{\mathrm{Cl},i} \sim N(0, \omega_{\mathrm{Cl}}^2)$: log-normal
individual parameters. The formula syntax covers more:

| formula | meaning |
|---|---|
| `Cl ~ 1 + (1 \| ID)` | random intercept per subject |
| `Cl ~ 1 + logWeight + (1 \| ID)` | a covariate, a fixed effect `Cl_logWeight` on a column of the table |
| `Ka + Cl ~ 1 + (1 \| p \| ID)` | the random effects of `Ka` and `Cl` correlated (same ID `p`) |
| `Cl ~ 1 + wt + (1 + dose \| p \| ID)` | a covariate and a random slope, correlated with the intercept |
| `Cl ~ 1 + (1 \| ID) + (1 \| ID:OCC)` | variability between subjects and between occasions of a subject |
| `Cl ~ 1 + (1 \| gr(ID, dist = laplace()))` | Laplace instead of normal random effects |

A group, a level of the grouping such as a subject, may own several conditions: its random
effects are shared by all of them. A condition outside every group, a reference without a
subject for example, has none. The random effects of one ID, or of one term without an ID, form a
block with a full covariance; different blocks are independent, so the covariance $\Omega$ is
block diagonal. Its parameters `omega_<a>_<b>` are the entries of a Cholesky factor of each
block, log standard deviations on the diagonal. Laplace, spike-and-slab and Dirichlet-process
random effects, deviations that are exactly zero unless the data need them, are the subject of
[chapter 8](guide-group-effects.html); they are fitted by `method = "focei"`, Dirichlet-process
ones also by `"saem"`. This chapter treats normal ones.

## Marginal likelihood

The random effects enter the model only through the parameter transformation. For subject $i$
with random effects $\eta_i$ the transformation gives the inner parameters
$\phi_i = h(\theta, \eta_i)$, the ODE and the observation function the prediction

$$\mu_{ij}(\theta, \eta_i) = g\bigl(x(t_{ij};\, \phi_i)\bigr),$$

and the observation model is

$$y_{ij} = \mu_{ij}(\theta, \eta_i) + \varepsilon_{ij}, \qquad
\varepsilon_{ij} \sim N\bigl(0, \sigma^2(\phi_i, t_{ij})\bigr), \qquad \eta_i \sim N(0, \Omega),$$

with the population parameters $\psi = (\theta, \Omega, \sigma)$. The right-hand side of the ODE
never sees $\eta_i$: the sensitivities of the prediction in the random effects come from the
chain rule through `g * x * p` as any other sensitivities, and the likelihood factorises over the
groups, since each $\eta_i$ couples only to the data $y_i$ of its group and to the population
through its prior. The marginal log-likelihood is

$$\ell(\psi) = \sum_{i=1}^N \log L_i(\psi), \qquad
L_i(\psi) = \int p(y_i \mid \eta_i, \psi)\, p(\eta_i \mid \Omega)\, \mathrm{d}\eta_i ,$$

with $y_i$ the data of all conditions of group $i$; the conditions without a group add their data
$-2 \log L$ as it is.

In code, the integrand is the objective of the data, `normL2(data, g * x * p, errmodel = e)`,
which gives $-2 \log p(y_i \mid \eta_i, \psi)$ summed over the conditions, plus the prior of the
random effects, $\sum_i \eta_i^\top \Omega^{-1} \eta_i + N \log \lvert \Omega \rvert$, which
`em()` builds from `randomEffects(p)`. Their sum is the joint $-2 \log$ density
$-2 \log p(y, \eta \mid \psi)$ up to a constant. `normT(data, g * x * p, errmodel = e, df = 4)`
instead of `normL2()` gives Student-t residuals with heavier tails.

## EM algorithm

The marginal likelihood couples the observed data $y$ and the latent random effects $\eta$. The
expectation-maximisation algorithm [@dempster1977maximum] maximises likelihoods of this form, and
every method of `em()` is an approximation of it.

### Lower bound

For a reference value $\psi^{(t)}$, let $q_i(\eta_i) = p(\eta_i \mid y_i, \psi^{(t)})$ be the
posterior of the random effects of group $i$. For any $\psi$, by Jensen's inequality,

$$\log L_i(\psi) = \log \int q_i(\eta_i)\, \frac{p(y_i, \eta_i \mid \psi)}{q_i(\eta_i)}\, \mathrm{d}\eta_i
\ge \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_i}\bigl[\log p(y_i, \eta_i \mid \psi)\bigr]}_{Q_i(\psi \mid \psi^{(t)})}
- \mathbb{E}_{q_i}\bigl[\log q_i(\eta_i)\bigr].$$

The bound is tight at $\psi = \psi^{(t)}$, where $p(y_i, \eta_i \mid \psi) / q_i(\eta_i) =
p(y_i \mid \psi^{(t)})$ is constant in $\eta_i$. The second term, the entropy of $q_i$, does not
depend on $\psi$. Summed over the groups, $Q(\psi \mid \psi^{(t)}) = \sum_i Q_i(\psi \mid
\psi^{(t)})$.

### Iteration

EM alternates two steps:

- E-step: at $\psi^{(t)}$, form the posteriors $q_i$ and with them $Q(\psi \mid \psi^{(t)})$ as a
  function of $\psi$.
- M-step: $\psi^{(t+1)} = \arg\max_\psi Q(\psi \mid \psi^{(t)})$.

The iteration never decreases the marginal likelihood. With $\mathcal{H}(q) = -\mathbb{E}_q \log
q$,

$$\ell(\psi^{(t+1)}) \ge Q(\psi^{(t+1)} \mid \psi^{(t)}) + \mathcal{H}(q)
\ge Q(\psi^{(t)} \mid \psi^{(t)}) + \mathcal{H}(q) = \ell(\psi^{(t)}),$$

the first inequality the bound at $\psi^{(t+1)}$, the second the M-step, the equality the
tightness at $\psi^{(t)}$. The improvement is strict unless $\psi^{(t)}$ is a stationary point of
$\ell$. Near the optimum EM converges linearly: the error shrinks per iteration by the fraction
of the information that is missing, the information of the random effects that the data do not
give [@dempster1977maximum].

When the M-step is itself hard but $\psi$ splits into blocks whose conditional maximisations are
easy, expectation conditional maximisation (ECM) [@meng1993maximum] replaces it by a sequence of
them, $\psi_A$ with $\psi_B$ held, then $\psi_B$ with the new $\psi_A$. Each step still increases
$Q$, so each cycle still increases $\ell$. For mixed-effects models the split is natural: the
covariance $\Omega$ has a closed-form conditional update from sufficient statistics, the
structural parameters do not.

### Three approximations

For a mixed-effects model,
$\log p(y_i, \eta_i \mid \psi) = \log p(y_i \mid \eta_i, \psi) + \log p(\eta_i \mid \Omega)$,
and the posterior $q_i \propto p(y_i \mid \eta_i, \psi^{(t)})\, p(\eta_i \mid \Omega^{(t)})$
runs through the nonlinear ODE solution and has no closed form; neither has the expectation
$Q_i$. The methods replace it by something computable:

- deterministic, low order: $q_i$ as a Gaussian at its mode and a one-point rule there. This is
  FOCEI, `method = "focei"`, and with an EM outer loop `method = "laplaceEM"`;
- deterministic, high order: a multi-point quadrature rule adapted to the Gaussian approximation
  of $q_i$, `method = "quadrature"`;
- stochastic: a Monte Carlo average over draws from $q_i$ by MCMC, averaged over the iterations
  rather than within them, `method = "saem"`.

## FOCEI

### Laplace approximation

Fix $\psi$ and write the joint $-2 \log$ density of group $i$ as

$$\Phi_i(\eta) = -2 \log p(y_i \mid \eta, \psi) - 2 \log p(\eta \mid \Omega).$$

With the conditional mode $\hat\eta_i = \arg\min_\eta \Phi_i(\eta)$ and $H_i = \nabla^2_\eta
\Phi_i(\hat\eta_i)$, the posterior precision is $P_i = H_i/2$. Expanding $\Phi_i$ to second order
around $\hat\eta_i$ and integrating the Gaussian gives Laplace's approximation of the $K$-dimensional
integral,

$$L_i(\psi) \approx (2\pi)^{K/2}\, \lvert P_i \rvert^{-1/2} \exp\bigl(-\tfrac12 \Phi_i(\hat\eta_i)\bigr),
\qquad -2 \log L_i \approx \Phi_i(\hat\eta_i) + \log \lvert H_i/2 \rvert - K \log(2\pi).$$

The prior term of $\Phi_i$ is written without its $K \log(2\pi)$, which cancels the last term, so
FOCEI minimises

$$F(\psi) = \sum_i \Bigl[ \Phi_i(\hat\eta_i) + \log \lvert H_i/2 \rvert \Bigr]$$

plus the data of the conditions without a group: the full $-2 \log L$ with every constant of the
data. $\log \lvert H_i/2 \rvert$ is the volume term. The "I" of FOCEI, first-order conditional
estimation with interaction [@wang2007derivation; @pinheiro1995approximations], is the
interaction between the random effects and the residual error: $H_i$ contains the derivatives of
$\sigma$ in $\eta$, which couple the structural and the error-model contributions. Without it
the method loses accuracy wherever $\sigma$ depends on $\eta$, as for a proportional or combined
error model.

In the language of EM, FOCEI approximates the posterior by the Gaussian
$N(\hat\eta_i, P_i^{-1})$ and the expectation by a single evaluation at $\hat\eta_i$ with the
normalising factor $\log \lvert P_i \rvert$; the M-step becomes one optimisation of the analytic
surrogate $F$ over all of $\psi$:

| EM | FOCEI |
|---|---|
| posterior $q_i$ | Gaussian at $\hat\eta_i$ with covariance $(H_i/2)^{-1}$ |
| E-step expectation | one point at $\hat\eta_i$, corrected by $\log \lvert H_i/2 \rvert$ |
| M-step | trust region on $F(\psi)$ with its exact gradient |

The conditional standard errors of the random effects that a fit reports are the square roots of
the diagonal of $P_i^{-1} = 2 H_i^{-1}$.

### Bilevel optimisation

FOCEI nests two trust regions. Per evaluation of the outer objective at $\psi$:

1. **Modes.** One trust-region solve per group finds $\hat\eta_i(\psi)$ over the data of all its
   conditions. It starts from the modes of the previous outer iterate, moved to first order
   along the outer step where that shift stays within the first inner radius, and stops where the
   Gauss-Newton step $H_i^{-1} g_i$ is below `innerControl$steptol`; near the mode a Newton step
   whose change of value drowns in the error of the solver is accepted by a smaller gradient. The
   step model is the Gauss-Newton Hessian plus an SR1 correction learned from the gradients of the
   accepted steps, the curvature of the prediction in the random effects that Gauss-Newton leaves
   out, wherever the sum stays positive definite; $H_i$ itself stays Gauss-Newton. An eigenvalue
   floor, $\lambda_k(H_i) \leftarrow \max\bigl(\lambda_k(H_i), 10^{-10} \operatorname{tr}(H_i)/K\bigr)$,
   keeps $\log \lvert H_i \rvert$ defined where the local curvature is degenerate.
2. **Outer gradient.** $\hat\eta_i$ minimises $\Phi_i$, so by the envelope theorem its shift
   contributes nothing to the derivative of $\Phi_i(\hat\eta_i)$:

   $$\nabla_\psi F = \sum_i \nabla_\psi \Phi_i \big|_{\eta = \hat\eta_i} + \sum_i \frac{\mathrm{d} \log \lvert H_i \rvert}{\mathrm{d} \psi}.$$

   The gradient $g_i$ in the random effects that the inner search leaves is of the order of
   `steptol` times the curvature; the first term takes the Newton correction to the exact mode,
   $-\Phi_i^{\psi\eta} H_i^{-1} g_i$, with which its error is of second order.
3. **Outer Hessian.** The model Hessian of the outer trust region is the Schur complement of the
   joint Hessian at the modes,

   $$\nabla^2_\psi F \approx \sum_i \Bigl[ \Phi_i^{\psi\psi} - \Phi_i^{\psi\eta} \bigl(\Phi_i^{\eta\eta}\bigr)^{-1} \Phi_i^{\eta\psi} \Bigr],$$

   in its Gauss-Newton form, plus the Hessian of the volume term where the model has the
   second-order sensitivities; an SR1 correction from the outer gradients of the last three
   accepted points learns what this model leaves out, negative curvature included, so the outer
   model may be indefinite.
4. **Outer step.** The outer trust region takes the step on $F(\psi)$, the modes are kept as
   starts for the next evaluation, and the loop repeats. A rejected step shrinks the radius to a
   quarter of the radius or of the step, whichever is shorter, in the inner and the outer trust
   region alike. The fit ends where its model can gain less than `trustControl$mtol` in the
   largest region `rmax`, so that a region shrunk by rejections does not end it, or, as in
   `trust()`, after five rejected trials in a row that leave the value flat within `ftol`: the
   error of the evaluation, typically that of the ODE solver, leaves nothing to resolve.

The bilevel loop runs in C++. The inner trust region of a group evaluates the residuals of each
of its conditions, the Gauss-Newton Hessian with the contribution of $\partial \sigma / \partial
\eta$ and the normal prior without a call of `normL2()`, and the trial points of all groups go
out as one batched prediction per round. Models with several outputs and error models that depend
on $\eta$ run through the same loop.

### Volume term

The inner Hessian has the Gauss-Newton form, over the data rows $r$ of the group with the Hessian
$L_r$ of the row loss in prediction and sigma,

$$H_i = \sum_r J_r^\top L_r J_r + 2\, \Omega^{-1}, \qquad J_r = \partial(\mu_r, \sigma_r) / \partial \eta ,$$

so the inner solve does not deliver the derivative of $\log \lvert H_i \rvert$. FOCEI evaluates
it in closed form,

$$\frac{\mathrm{d} \log \lvert H_i \rvert}{\mathrm{d} \psi_k}
= \operatorname{tr}\Bigl(H_i^{-1} \frac{\partial H_i}{\partial \psi_k}\Big|_\eta\Bigr)
+ \sum_l \operatorname{tr}\Bigl(H_i^{-1} \frac{\partial H_i}{\partial \eta_l}\Bigr) \frac{\mathrm{d} \hat\eta_l}{\mathrm{d} \psi_k},$$

with $\mathrm{d}\hat\eta / \mathrm{d}\psi = -(\Phi_i^{\eta\eta})^{-1} \Phi_i^{\eta\psi}$ from the
implicit function theorem on the exact joint Hessian. $\partial H_i / \partial \psi_k$ needs the
mixed second derivatives $\partial^2 \mu / (\partial \eta\, \partial \psi_k)$, and
$\partial H_i / \partial \eta_l$ the second derivatives $\partial^2 \mu / (\partial \eta\,
\partial \eta_l)$, the same for $\sigma$; the Gauss-Newton form needs no third-order
sensitivities. The Hessian of the volume term leaves out the third-order sensitivities and
$\mathrm{d}^2 \hat\eta / \mathrm{d}\psi^2$. In the direction of $\Omega$ that is a large error
when $\sigma$ depends on $\eta$; there the Hessian of the quadrature fit is the better one.

`control$derivMode` decides how FOCEI gets the second derivatives:

- `"forward-reverse"`, the default, for models built with
  `derivMode = c("forward", "reverse", "forward-reverse")`. Every second derivative the volume term
  uses is a contraction, a trace $\operatorname{tr}(M\, \partial H_i / \partial x)$ with a fixed
  matrix $M$ or the joint Hessian applied to a direction of the random effects, and comes from one
  forward pass along the random effects and a backward sweep with seeds on the predictions and
  sigmas of the data rows; [chapter 3](guide-sensitivities.html) describes the sweeps. The volume
  gradient is exact; the curvature of the volume term is learned by the SR1 correction along the
  steps taken.
- `"forward-forward"`, the second-order sensitivities of models built with `deriv2 = TRUE`, which
  give the exact Hessian of the volume term to the outer model as well.

A model with only one of the two takes it, with a message. The Hessian a fit reports, from which
the standard errors come, is the exact one, forward over forward, where the model has `deriv2`;
otherwise the exact Schur complement of the joint Hessian, up to 500 parameters, with the volume
curvature of the variance parameters, which is exact for models linear in the random effects.
`summary()` says which. `control = list(secondOrderCorrection = FALSE)` drops the derivative of
the volume term altogether, which biases the estimates.

### Fit

`init` holds the parameters that are neither random effects nor created by the effect formulas,
which start at 0; the standard deviations of the random effects start at `control$sd`.

```{r}
init <- c(Ka = 0, V = 3, Cl = 0.7, sigma = log(0.5))
fit <- em(obj = normL2(data, g * x * p, errmodel = e), random = random, init = init, verbose = FALSE)
summary(fit)
```

The hyperparameters `omega_*` are log standard deviations of the random effects, shown on their
natural scale in the table of random effects. The shrinkage measures how much the data inform
the individual parameters: near 0 the modes spread as widely as the random effects, near 1 the
data of a subject hardly move its parameter.

`value` is $-2 \log L$ with every constant of the data; `valueNonmem`, $-2 \log L$ less
$N_{\text{obs}} \log(2\pi)$, compares with the `OBJ` of NONMEM. The fit holds the estimates in
`argument`, `Omega` and in `omega` the standard deviations and correlations with standard errors,
in `random` the modes of every group with their conditional standard errors, and `etaModes`,
`etaSE` and `shrinkage`. Its methods are those of a fit: `coef()`, `vcov()`, `confint()` (Wald, or
`method = "profile"`), `logLik()` and with it `AIC()` and `BIC()`, `anova()` of nested fits,
`predict()` (individual and population predictions), `residuals()`, `simulate()` and the plots
below.

### Settings

| entry of `control` | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `sd` | `0.3` | start of the random-effect standard deviations not given in `init` |
| `innerControl` | `rinit = 1`, `rmax = 10`, `iterlim = 30`, `steptol = 1e-8`, `mtol = 1e-12` | the trust region of the modes |
| `trustControl` | `rinit = 1`, `rmax = 10`, `iterlim = 200`, `ftol = 1e-7`, `mtol = 1e-5` | the trust region of the population parameters |
| `derivMode` | `"forward-reverse"` | the second derivatives of the volume term, or `"forward-forward"` |
| `secondOrderCorrection` | `TRUE` | the derivative of the volume term |

`fixed` holds parameters at given values. `em(cores = )` spreads the groups and conditions over
threads, `sparse = TRUE` fits large models with many fixed effects on sparse Hessians, the Schur
complement and the volume term of every group local to its parameters; `"auto"` decides as
`trust()` does. The inner tolerances are tight, since errors in the modes pass into the volume
term and the outer gradient; the outer `mtol` is that of a fit, a predicted change of $10^{-5}$ in
$-2 \log L$. As in any fit, the solver error has to stay below these tolerances.

## Adaptive sparse-grid quadrature

### Beyond Laplace

The Laplace approximation replaces the integral

$$L_i(\psi) = \int e^{-\frac12 \Phi_i(\eta; \psi)}\, \mathrm{d}\eta$$

by one evaluation at $\hat\eta_i$ with a curvature correction: it treats $\Phi_i$ as quadratic.
Its error is dominated by the third and fourth derivatives of $\Phi_i$ at the mode and is
$O(K/n_i)$ per group with $n_i$ data points. It matters for informative but short trajectories,
such as oral doses sampled near the absorption limit, where $\Phi_i$ is skewed, and where the
variance components are the target of the inference: the approximation weights the peak against
the tails differently from the integral, which biases $\Omega$. A cubature rule

$$\int e^{-\frac12 \Phi_i(\eta)}\, \mathrm{d}\eta \approx \sum_{b=1}^{B} W_b\, e^{-\frac12 \Phi_i(\eta_b)}$$

with nodes $\eta_b$ and weights $W_b$ removes that error step by step: it is exact when the
integrand is a polynomial of bounded degree times a Gaussian, contains Laplace as its one-node
case, and converges at a rate the smoothness of $\Phi_i$ sets. The rules below keep the number
$B$ of nodes polynomial in the number $K$ of random effects.

### Nested rules

The Gauss-Hermite rule with $m$ nodes,

$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(z)\, e^{-z^2}\, \mathrm{d}z \approx \sum_{j=1}^m w_j\, g(z_j),$$

is exact for polynomials $g$ of degree up to $2m - 1$, but its node sets of different sizes do
not contain each other. Genz and Keister [@genz1996fully] extend the three-point rule by
Kronrod-Patterson steps to a nested sequence of 1, 3, 9, 19 and 35 points, exact to degree 1, 5,
15, 29 and 51: every rule holds the nodes of the previous one, so a higher level reuses every
evaluation of the lower one. dMod2 computes the nodes and weights once, in 300-bit arithmetic.

### Smolyak combination

The tensor product of one-dimensional rules puts a node at every combination of their nodes. It
is exact in each coordinate separately but needs $m^K$ nodes: 16807 ODE solves per group and
evaluation for $K = 5$ and $m = 7$. A polynomial of total degree $d$ has far fewer monomials than
the full product space, and the sparse grid of Smolyak [@smolyak1963quadrature] pays only for
those. With $\Delta^l = \mathcal{U}^l - \mathcal{U}^{l-1}$ the difference of the one-dimensional
rules of levels $l$ and $l - 1$, the rule of level $L \ge K$ is

$$A(L, K) = \sum_{\lvert \mathbf{i} \rvert \le L} \Delta^{i_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \Delta^{i_K},$$

where $\mathbf{i} = (i_1, \dots, i_K)$ sets how many nodes go into each coordinate. Heiss and
Winschel [@heiss2008likelihood] developed such rules for the likelihood of random-coefficient
models, and Clausen, Rønn and Skovgaard [@clausen2009maximum] applied adaptive sparse-grid
quadrature to nonlinear mixed-effects models. dMod2 differentiates the rule exactly through the
sensitivities of the ODE, gradient and Hessian of the marginal likelihood included. The level is
the one accuracy setting:

- $A(L, K)$ integrates every polynomial of total degree $2(L - K) + 1$ exactly against the
  Gaussian weight.
- The number of nodes grows polynomially in $K$ at fixed $L - K$. For $K = 3$ the levels 3 to 7
  have 1, 7, 19, 45 and 117 nodes; for $K = 4$ the levels 6 and 7 have 29 and 89, against 49 and
  201 for a grid of non-nested Gauss-Hermite rules.
- At $L = K$ the rule is a single node, which after the change of variables below is Laplace's
  approximation. Each level above it probes more of the tails.

The differences of the rules make some weights $W_b$ negative; polynomial exactness holds for the
signed combination. The log-likelihood of a group,
$\log L_i \approx \log \bigl\lvert \sum_b W_b\, e^{-\frac12 \Phi_i(\eta_b)} \bigr\rvert$, is
therefore summed in log space with the signs kept, as below.

### Adaptation

The rule integrates against the weight $\exp(-z^\top z)$ in a standard frame; the integral of
group $i$ lives around its mode. The local Gaussian $N(\hat\eta_i, P_i^{-1})$, $P_i = H_i/2$, of
FOCEI matches $\Phi_i$ to second order at the mode, and as the map from $z$ to $\eta$ it makes the
quadrature adaptive: every outer iterate gives new $(\hat\eta_i, P_i)$, the nodes follow, and the
rule stays centred as $\psi$ moves. With $L_H$ the lower Cholesky factor of $P_i$, the change of
variables

$$\eta = \hat\eta_i + \sqrt{2}\, L_H^{-\top} z$$

maps a standard normal in $z$ onto $N(\hat\eta_i, P_i^{-1})$; the $\sqrt 2$ converts between the
weight $e^{-z^2}$ of the rule and $e^{-z^2/2}$. Its Jacobian $2^{K/2} / \lvert \det L_H \rvert$
and the factor $\exp(z^\top z)$ that undoes the weight of the rule go into the weights,

$$\log \lvert W_b \rvert = \tfrac{K}{2} \log 2 - \log \lvert \det L_H \rvert + \log \lvert w_b \rvert + z_b^\top z_b ,$$

with the sign of the rule weight $w_b$ kept apart. The rule is then exact when
$e^{-\Phi_i/2}$ is a polynomial in $\eta$ times the local Gaussian, and at $L = K$ it is a single
node at $\hat\eta_i$ with the Laplace normaliser as weight.

### Signed log-sum-exp

For the nodes $b = 1, \dots, B$ of a group let $\ell_b = \log \lvert W_b \rvert - \frac12
\Phi_i(\eta_b)$ and $s_b = \operatorname{sgn}(W_b)$. Then

$$\log L_i = \log \Bigl\lvert \sum_b s_b\, e^{\ell_b} \Bigr\rvert
= \ell_{\max} + \log \Bigl\lvert \sum_b s_b\, e^{\ell_b - \ell_{\max}} \Bigr\rvert, \qquad
\ell_{\max} = \max_b \ell_b ,$$

and the moments of the posterior use the normalised weights with their signs,

$$\tilde w_b = s_b\, e^{\ell_b - \log L_i}, \qquad \hat m_i = \sum_b \tilde w_b\, \eta_b, \qquad
\hat M_i = \sum_b \tilde w_b\, \eta_b \eta_b^\top .$$

A sum $\sum_b s_b e^{\ell_b - \ell_{\max}}$ that is not positive or not finite means the grid does
not resolve the posterior: the evaluation stops and names the group, and a higher level resolves it.
The effective sample size $1 / \sum_b \tilde w_b^2$ of every group is part of the diagnostics.

The gradient of the marginal log-likelihood is the weighted average of the node gradients, and
its Hessian follows from the log-sum-exp identity,

$$\nabla_\psi \log L_i = \sum_b \tilde w_b\, \nabla_\psi \ell_b, \qquad
\nabla^2_\psi \log L_i = \sum_b \tilde w_b\, \nabla^2_\psi \ell_b + \operatorname{Cov}_{\tilde w}(\nabla_\psi \ell_b),$$

with $\nabla_\psi \ell_b = -\frac12 \nabla_\psi \Phi_i(\eta_b)$ and the covariance taken under the
signed weights, $\operatorname{Cov}(g) = \mathbb{E}[g g^\top] - \mathbb{E}[g]\, \mathbb{E}[g]^\top$;
the identity uses only that the weights sum to one. The node gradients and Hessians come from one
prediction over all groups, nodes and conditions, through the sensitivities of the chain.

### Frozen nodes

The fit alternates between placing the grid and optimising on it:

1. **Rebuild.** At the current $\psi$ the inner trust region of FOCEI finds every
   $\hat\eta_i(\psi)$ and $H_i$, and the adapted grid of each group is placed. The level of a
   group is the lowest from its stage up whose next level changes its $-2 \log L_i$ by at most
   `tol` over the number of groups; levels are never lowered, so the objective stays smooth.
2. **Step.** One trust-region run over every parameter, structural and Cholesky, on the frozen
   nodes, with the exact Hessian where the model has second derivatives. The nodes of the
   mu-referenced fixed effects, random intercepts whose formula covers every condition with data
   and covariates constant within a group, are frozen in $\phi_i = D_i \beta + \eta_i$: their data
   term does not depend on $\beta$ between rebuilds, so they need no sensitivities, and the frozen
   nodes stay accurate over larger steps.
3. **End of a stage.** A stage ends when a Newton step on the rebuilt nodes would lower
   $-2 \log L$ by less than `tolDecrement`, or by less than the nodes resolve: the change of
   $-2 \log L$ by the next level, summed over the groups. With the levels capped by `maxLevel`
   this resolution can stay above `tolDecrement`, and a step on frozen nodes then gains less than
   the rebuild moves. A step that raised $-2 \log L$ on rebuilt nodes of the same levels by more
   than a Newton step would gain also ends the stage, at its iterate of lowest $-2 \log L$.

`method = "quadrature"` first runs FOCEI to convergence and starts from its $\psi$ and modes.

At the estimate an importance-sampling check certifies every group: a multivariate $t_5$ proposal
at the mode and conditional covariance, evaluated on randomly shifted lattice points, gives
$-2 \log L_i$ with a standard error and the Pareto shape of its weights [@vehtari2024pareto]. A
group is flagged when the two values differ by more than three standard errors plus the error its
level allows, or when the Pareto shape exceeds 0.7.

| entry of `control$quadrature` | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `tol` | `0.1` | allowed change of $-2 \log L$ by the next level, split over the groups; `Inf` keeps the levels of the stages |
| `levels` | `K + 1` | the stages; level `K + s` integrates polynomials of total degree `2 s + 1` exactly |
| `maxLevel` | `K + 8` | highest level |
| `tolDecrement` | `1e-4` | Newton decrement that ends a stage |
| `maxEcmPerStage` | `10` | rebuilds per stage |
| `cm1Control`, `maxCm1Iter` | `rinit = 1`, `ftol = mtol = 1e-8`; `30` | `trust()` settings and iterations of a step |
| `pruneTol` | `Inf` | drop nodes whose weight lies this much in log below the largest |
| `certificate` | `points = 256`, `seed = 1` | the importance-sampling check, `FALSE` to skip it |

A quadrature fit holds `stageTrace`, one row per rebuild with the stage level, the value, the
Newton decrement, the resolution, the highest level and the number of nodes; `etaCov`, the
posterior covariance $\hat M_i - \hat m_i \hat m_i^\top$ of every group; and `certificate`.
`plotTrace(fit)` draws the trace, and `plotRandomEffects(fit)` the histograms of the modes over the
fitted $N(0, \Omega_{kk})$.

## Laplace EM

`method = "laplaceEM"` maximises the marginal likelihood by ECM. Its CM-1 step moves the
structural parameters by a trust-region run on frozen nodes of level $K + 1$, the rule of degree 3
around the modes; a single node would lose the posterior variance. Its CM-2 step is the
closed-form update of $\Omega$.

The complete-data log-density of the random effects is

$$\log p(\eta \mid \Omega) = -\tfrac12 \sum_i \Bigl[ \log \lvert \Omega \rvert + \eta_i^\top \Omega^{-1} \eta_i \Bigr] + \text{const}.$$

Its expectation under the posteriors replaces $\eta_i \eta_i^\top$ by the posterior second moment
$M_i$, and setting the derivative in $\Omega$ to zero gives the sufficient statistic

$$S = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N M_i .$$

Per block of $\Omega$ the maximiser is the block of $S$ itself, and its Cholesky factor gives the
parameters `omega_<a>_<b>`; with some entries fixed the update maximises over the others. Laplace
EM takes the moments of the Laplace approximation, $M_i = \hat\eta_i \hat\eta_i^\top + (H_i/2)^{-1}$:
the mode alone would leave out the posterior covariance and shrink $\Omega$.

EM converges linearly, so the change of the parameters per iteration says little about the
distance to the fixed point. With $\delta_t = \max \lvert \psi^{(t)} - \psi^{(t-1)} \rvert$ and the
rate $\rho = \delta_t / \delta_{t-1}$, the remaining distance is about $\delta_t \rho / (1 - \rho)$,
and the fit stops when both lie below `epsEcm` (default `1e-5`), after at most `maxEcm` (default
200) iterations. The value it reports is the quadrature at level $K + 2$. It reads `epsEcm`,
`maxEcm`, `cm1Control` and `maxCm1Iter` from `control$quadrature`.

## SAEM

### Stochastic E-step

FOCEI and the sparse grid are deterministic approximations of the same expectation, both built on
the local Gaussian. FOCEI is biased wherever the posterior is not Gaussian; the grid resolves such
a posterior only at higher levels, whose number of nodes grows faster the larger $K$, and every
node costs an ODE solve. A draw $\eta_i \sim q_i$ needs no Gaussian assumption and costs the same
whatever $K$. The E-step becomes an estimate with a variance, and $\ell$ need not increase in
every iteration.

Monte Carlo EM replaces $Q_i$ by an average over $M$ draws. Its error must vanish for the
iteration to converge, so $M$ has to grow without bound, and every draw is discarded at the end of
its iteration. Stochastic-approximation EM [@delyon1999convergence] averages across iterations
instead of within them: very few draws per iteration, a single one even, accumulated by a
Robbins-Monro recursion [@robbins1951stochastic], so the Monte Carlo error is averaged out along
the trajectory rather than at each point of it.

### Sufficient statistics

The recursion rests on the exponential-family structure of the random effects. If the
complete-data likelihood is of the form

$$\log p(y, \eta \mid \psi) = -\varphi(\psi) + \bigl\langle S(y, \eta),\, \nu(\psi) \bigr\rangle$$

with a sufficient statistic $S$, the E-step needs only the vector $\mathbb{E}_q[S(y, \eta)]$, and
the M-step is a fixed map $s \mapsto \hat\psi(s)$. The expectation of a fixed statistic is what a
Robbins-Monro recursion estimates:

$$s_k = s_{k-1} + \gamma_k \bigl( S(y, \eta^{(k)}) - s_{k-1} \bigr), \qquad
\eta^{(k)} \sim q(\cdot \mid \psi^{(k-1)}), \qquad \psi^{(k)} = \hat\psi(s_k).$$

Under the conditions on $\gamma_k$ below, $s_k$ converges almost surely and the iterates converge to
a stationary point of $\ell$ [@delyon1999convergence; @kuhn2004coupling].

The block of the random effects fits this form exactly. With $\eta_i \sim N(0, \Omega)$,

$$\log p(\eta \mid \Omega) = -\tfrac{N}{2} \log \lvert \Omega \rvert
- \tfrac12 \Bigl\langle \sum_i \eta_i \eta_i^\top,\, \Omega^{-1} \Bigr\rangle + \text{const},$$

with the statistic $\sum_i \eta_i \eta_i^\top$, and the M-step is the closed form of Laplace EM
with the outer product of a draw in place of the posterior moment. A fixed effect $\beta$ that
enters a symbol only through $\phi_i = D_i \beta + \eta_i$, with $D_i$ constant within the group,
is mu-referenced: holding $\phi_i$ while $\beta$ moves, the data term does not depend on $\beta$,
and $\beta$ and $\Omega$ follow in closed form from averaged statistics of $\phi$, the
generalised least-squares $\beta$ alternated with the update of $\Omega$.

The other structural parameters, those of the error model and those without a random effect,
enter through the ODE solution and have no sufficient statistic of fixed dimension. During
burn-in they take one `trust()` step per iteration on the complete-data objective at the drawn
random effects. During averaging the gradient $g_k$ and Hessian $H_k$ of that objective at
$\theta_k$ enter a Robbins-Monro average of its quadratic models,

$$A_k = A_{k-1} + \gamma_k (H_k - A_{k-1}), \qquad c_k = c_{k-1} + \gamma_k (H_k \theta_k - g_k - c_{k-1}),$$

and $\theta$ takes the Newton step on $\frac12 \theta^\top A_k \theta - c_k^\top \theta$, at most
one unit long. At the fixed point the averaged gradient vanishes, which by Fisher's identity is
the score of the marginal likelihood. An average of the Newton steps of single draws would solve
$\mathbb{E}[H^{-1} g] = 0$ instead, which misses the score wherever the curvature differs between
draws; for a residual scale it moves the estimate towards the harmonic mean of the residual sums of
squares.

### Iteration

Each iteration $k$ has three steps:

- **Simulation.** For each group a draw $\eta_i^{(k)} \sim q_i(\eta \mid y_i, \psi^{(k-1)})$ with
  the target $\Phi_i$ of FOCEI, whose value for all groups comes from one prediction without
  sensitivities. A few random-walk Metropolis steps from the previous draw are followed by
  independence proposals from $N\bigl(\hat\eta_i, 1.5\, (H_i/2)^{-1}\bigr)$ at the conditional
  modes, refreshed every few iterations. Every proposal leaves $q_i$ invariant, so a short chain
  suffices [@kuhn2004coupling]. The random numbers come from the session stream, so `set.seed()`
  reproduces a fit.
- **Approximation.** The statistics of $\phi$ and $\eta$ are updated,
  $S \leftarrow S + \gamma_k (s(\eta^{(k)}) - S)$.
- **Maximisation.** $\beta$ and $\Omega$ in closed form from $S$, the other structural
  parameters by the step above.

### Burn-in and averaging

The step size $\gamma_k$ separates the two tasks of the algorithm. During burn-in $\gamma_k = 1$:
no memory, and the iterates move at full step towards the region of the optimum. The random-walk
steps adapt towards an acceptance rate of 0.4. Draws of chains that have not mixed yet
underestimate the spread of the random effects, so a variance of $\Omega$ shrinks by at most 5 %
per iteration, the simulated annealing of Lavielle [@lavielle2014mixed]. Burn-in ends when no
parameter drifts: the slope of every parameter over the last `window` iterations is below twice
its standard error.

During averaging $\gamma_k = k^{-0.7}$, counted from the end of burn-in, satisfies the
Robbins-Monro conditions $\sum_k \gamma_k = \infty$ and $\sum_k \gamma_k^2 < \infty$, and the
estimate is the mean of the iterates after the first `window` of the averaging
[@polyak1992acceleration]. Averaging ends, after at least `2 * window` iterations, when the
expected increase of $-2 \log L$ from the Monte Carlo error of the estimate is below `mcTol`,

$$\mathbb{E}\bigl[\Delta(-2 \log L)\bigr] \approx \operatorname{tr}\bigl(I_c\, V\, I_c\, I_{\text{obs}}^{-1}\bigr),$$

with $V$ the batch-means covariance of the M-steps of the single draws, $I_c$ the complete-data
information and $I_{\text{obs}}$ half the Hessian of the marginal by quadrature at the end of
burn-in. `converged` reports both rules; `nBurnin` and `nEM` are maxima.

### Cost

SAEM removes the bias of Laplace and the growth of the grid, and pays in three places:

- **No monotone improvement.** The guarantee of EM needs the exact E-step; the convergence of SAEM
  is asymptotic and almost sure, not per iteration. A trace that goes the wrong way for a while is
  no failure.
- **No value from the algorithm.** SAEM never forms the marginal likelihood, only the
  complete-data objective. `em()` evaluates the marginal once, at the estimate, by quadrature of
  level $K + 2$, so `value` compares with those of FOCEI and of the quadrature.
- **Standard errors from that evaluation**, from the Hessian of the quadrature, not from a
  stochastic approximation of the information along the path.

SAEM is the method for many random effects, strongly nonlinear models and posteriors that are
skewed, heavy-tailed or multimodal [@kuhn2005maximum].

| entry of `control$saem` | default | controls |
|---|---|---|
| `nBurnin`, `nEM` | `200`, `300` | most burn-in and averaging iterations |
| `nMcmc`, `nLaplace` | `3`, `3` | random-walk and independence steps per iteration |
| `laplaceEvery` | `5` | iterations between refreshes of the conditional modes |
| `laplaceScale` | `1.5` | factor of the covariance of the independence proposal |
| `window` | `25` | iterations of the drift test and of the averaging start |
| `mcTol` | `0.05` | expected increase of $-2 \log L$ from the Monte Carlo error that ends the averaging |

## Methods compared

The same model fitted by the four methods, from the same start:

```{r}
obj <- normL2(data, g * x * p, errmodel = e)
fits <- list(focei = fit,
             quadrature = em(obj, random, init, method = "quadrature", verbose = FALSE),
             saem = em(obj, random, init, method = "saem", verbose = FALSE))
round(sapply(fits, function(f) c(f$argument[names(fit$argument)], minus2logL = f$value)), 3)
```

```{r}
laplaceEM <- em(obj, random, init, method = "laplaceEM", verbose = FALSE)
round(c(laplaceEM$argument[names(fit$argument)], minus2logL = laplaceEM$value), 3)
```

The estimates agree within their standard errors. The values of $-2 \log L$ differ by the
accuracy of their approximations of the same integral; Laplace EM and SAEM report the quadrature
at their estimates. The stage trace of the quadrature fit has one row per rebuild, and its
certificate the importance-sampling check of every group:

```{r}
fits$quadrature$stageTrace[, c("level", "ecmIter", "OFV", "decrement", "resolution", "maxLevel", "nodes")]
fits$quadrature$certificate
```

`r q <- fits$quadrature$stageTrace; if (nrow(q) == 1 && q$decrement[1] < q$resolution[1]) "Here one rebuild ends the fit: the Newton decrement on the rebuilt nodes lies below what the nodes resolve, so the estimate of FOCEI stands, with the value of the quadrature." else sprintf("Here the fit takes %d rebuilds.", nrow(q))` `r flagged <- sum(fits$quadrature$certificate$flag); if (flagged == 0) "No group is flagged." else sprintf("%d of %d groups are flagged.", flagged, nrow(fits$quadrature$certificate))` `plotTrace()` draws the trace of a fit with
several rebuilds.

## Diagnostics

Conditional weighted residuals (CWRES) linearise the model around the modes; normalised
prediction distribution errors (NPDE) come from simulations of the fitted model, decorrelated
per subject, and do not depend on a linearisation. Both should look like standard normal noise
against the prediction and against time.

```{r, fig.height = 6}
plotResiduals(fit, type = c("CWRES", "NPDE"), nsim = 200, seed = 1)
```

The visual predictive check compares percentiles of the data with prediction intervals from the
simulations, per time bin.

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
plotVPC(fit, nsim = 200, bins = 8, seed = 1)
```

Random effects plotted against a covariate show whether it explains part of the variability:

```{r, fig.height = 3.5}
plotRandomEffects(fit, covariates = table["weight"])
```

## Covariates

Clearance and volume usually scale with body weight. The weight enters as a fixed effect on a
column of the table, centred on the log scale:

```{r}
table$logWeight <- log(table$weight / 70)
trafo2 <- branch(define(NULL, "x <- x", x = c("Ka", "V", "Cl", "Ag", "Cc", "sigma")), table = table) |>
  insert("Ag <- dose", dose = dose) |>
  insert("Cc <- 0") |>
  insert("x <- exp(x)", x = c("Ka", "V", "Cl", "sigma")) |>
  insert(Ka + V ~ 1 + (1 | ID)) |>
  insert(Cl ~ 1 + logWeight + (1 | ID))
p2 <- P(trafo2, method = "explicit", modelname = "theo_p2", compile = FALSE, deriv2 = TRUE, derivMode = dm)
compile(p2, output = "theo2")
fit2 <- em(normL2(data, g * x * p2, errmodel = e), randomEffects(p2), init, verbose = FALSE)
comparison <- anova(fit, fit2)
comparison
```

`anova()` compares the nested fits by the likelihood ratio. Here the weight lowers $-2 \log L$ by
`r round(comparison$chisq[2], 2)`, with a p-value of `r round(comparison$p[2], 2)`: among twelve
subjects of similar weight it explains little of the spread of the clearance, and the simpler
model stays.

## Nested and crossed groups

Random effects over several groupings, nested like occasions within subjects or crossed like
patients and centres, are written as further terms of the formula. `em()` integrates them per
connected component of the conditions, by FOCEI; the [pharmacometrics project](pharmacometrics.html)
fits mavoglurant with variability between occasions this way:

```r
insert(trafo, Cl ~ 1 + (1 | ID) + (1 | ID:OCC))
```

Which groups differ at all, rather than by how much, is the subject of
[chapter 8](guide-group-effects.html).

## Multistart

Like any fit, a mixed-effects fit can end in a local optimum. `msem()` runs `em()` from `fits`
starts, perturbed around `init` with the standard deviation `sd`, and returns the best fit with
all starts in `$multistart`. `theophyllineMultistart.R` of the example project `pharmacometrics`
runs 200 starts for each of FOCEI, quadrature and SAEM, from the same draws:

```{r, include = FALSE, purl = FALSE}
project <- normalizePath("../../examples/pharmacometrics")
stored <- file.exists(file.path(project, "results", "multistart.rds"))
knitr::read_chunk("../../examples/pharmacometrics/theophyllineMultistart.R")
```

```{r multistart, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !stored}
cat("> Results pending: `results/multistart.rds` of the project is written by `theophyllineMultistart.R`.\n")
```

The waterfalls, one per method, sort the starts by $-2 \log L$, drawn over the range of the two best
plateaus:

```{r, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 3.5, eval = stored}
saved <- readRDS(file.path(project, "results", "multistart.rds"))
waterfall <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(saved$multistart), function(m) {
  starts <- saved$multistart[[m]]
  data.frame(method = factor(m, names(saved$multistart)), rank = rank(starts$value, ties.method = "first"),
             value = starts$value, converged = starts$converged)
}))
ggplot2::ggplot(waterfall, ggplot2::aes(rank, value, colour = converged)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 1) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~method, nrow = 1) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = min(waterfall$value, na.rm = TRUE) + c(-1, 20)) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "black", `FALSE` = dMod_colors[2]),
                               labels = c(`TRUE` = "yes", `FALSE` = "no")) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "start, sorted by value", y = "-2 log L", colour = "converged") +
  theme_dMod()
```

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = stored}
lowest <- vapply(saved$multistart, function(t) sum(t$value < min(t$value, na.rm = TRUE) + 1, na.rm = TRUE), 0)
```

`r if (stored) sum(waterfall$value > min(waterfall$value, na.rm = TRUE) + 20, na.rm = TRUE) else "?"`
of the `r if (stored) nrow(waterfall) else "?"` starts end more than 20 above the best and lie
outside the plot. All three methods find the same two optima, $-2 \log L$ shifted by their
approximations. Most starts end on the upper plateau, the fit of the sections above; about
`r if (stored) round(mean(lowest)) else "?"` of 200 per method reach the lower one, the flip-flop
solution:

```{r, eval = stored}
flipflop <- saved$best$FOCEI
signif(rbind(fit = c(exp(fit$argument[c("Ka", "V", "Cl")]), minus2logL = fit$value),
             flipflop = c(exp(flipflop[c("Ka", "V", "Cl")]),
                          minus2logL = min(saved$multistart$FOCEI$value, na.rm = TRUE))), 4)
```

With one oral dose and no intravenous data, the absorption rate `Ka` and the elimination rate
`Cl / V` can swap. In the flip-flop solution the absorption is the slow step, the volume shrinks
to `r if (stored) round(exp(flipflop[["V"]]), 1) else "?"` L and the random effect of `Ka`
vanishes. The likelihood prefers it by
`r if (stored) round(fit$value - min(saved$multistart$FOCEI$value, na.rm = TRUE), 1) else "?"`,
but a volume of a few litres is not that of theophylline, which spreads through the body water,
about 0.5 L/kg. Knowledge of the drug, or a prior on `V`, decides for the upper plateau.

### A variance at its boundary

At the flip-flop solution the data leave no variation of `Ka` between the subjects, and its
variance runs to 0, which lies at minus infinity on the log scale of the hyperparameters and which
no method reaches. `em()` checks every normal random effect of its own block whose standard
deviation ends below 0.1. It fits the model again without that random effect, its etas fixed at 0,
from the estimates, and where this raises $-2 \log L$ by at most
`control$boundary` (default 0.1) it returns that fit, with the variance set to 0 and named in
`boundary`. On the lower plateau every method sets the variance of `Ka` to 0:

```{r, eval = stored}
sapply(saved$multistart, function(t) sum(t$boundary == "omega_Ka_Ka"))
sapply(saved$best, function(b) signif(b[c("Ka", "V", "Cl")], 4))
```

The lower $-2 \log L$ of FOCEI is its approximation error, not a better optimum.
`theophyllineMultistart.R` refits the best fit of every method by every other method from its
estimates:

```{r crosscheck, eval = FALSE}
```

```{r, eval = stored}
saved$cross
```

From every starting point each method ends at the same flip-flop estimates and reports its own
$-2 \log L$ there: FOCEI about 1.5 below the quadrature, which integrates the random effects more
accurately than Laplace's method; SAEM, valued by the quadrature of level $K + 2$ at its estimate,
within a few tenths of the quadrature.

`msem()` draws every start and seed before the fits are spread over `cores`, so `set.seed()`
reproduces a run; `cores = c(fits = , conditions = )` splits the cores between parallel fits and
threads inside each, as in `mstrust()`. The fit from `init` runs first, and every other start ends
after `budget` (default 5) times its outer iterations; `budget = Inf` lets every start run to
convergence. `plotValues()` draws `$multistart` as a waterfall.

## Summary

- Random effects are declared by effect formulas in `insert()` on a branched transformation, on
  the scale the transformation gives the symbol.
- Every method of `em()` is an approximation of EM for the same marginal likelihood: FOCEI by
  Laplace's method at the modes with the exact derivative of the volume term, the quadrature by
  adaptive sparse grids around the modes, Laplace EM by ECM on the Laplace approximation, SAEM by
  Metropolis draws averaged by a Robbins-Monro recursion.
- Build the model with `deriv2 = TRUE` and `derivMode = c("forward", "reverse", "forward-reverse")`.
- Check fits with CWRES, NPDE and the VPC, and covariates against the random effects.

## References
